title: VideoLoom: Joint Spatial-Temporal Video Understanding
one_liner: Train a video model on a dataset of precise character locations and timing labels so it learns to reason about what happens where and when at the same time.
lead: Video LLMs (models trained to answer questions about video) usually stumble when you ask them to find something in both space and time together. Most approaches excel at tracking objects moving through the scene or understanding a sequence of events, but not both at once. VideoLoom fixes this by training on a carefully labeled dataset where every caption pins down exactly where in the frame and when in the video each character appears.

problem.h2: Video models split the work and lose the connection
paras: When you watch a video, you naturally see where things happen and when they happen as one picture. Your brain says: that person entered from the left at the 3-second mark and walked to the right by 5 seconds.

Video models today usually treat these two questions separately. One part of the model asks: what is moving across the frame (space)? Another part asks: what changes from frame to frame (time)? When you ask the finished model to find a person in a specific spot during a specific moment, it stumbles because the parts never practiced thinking jointly.

A beginner might try to just train on a bigger video dataset and hope the model learns both skills. That fails because videos in the wild do not come with precise location and time labels. The model has no clear signal that says: this caption describes something that happens here and there, not everywhere or just in one frame.

callout.html: Teach a video model to find characters by training on a dataset where every caption says exactly where and when in the video that character appears.

panels.title: 1. Old approach: space and time apart
panels.caption: Two paths process video, ignore each other.

panels.title: 2. Ask a joint question
panels.caption: Where is the character at 3 seconds?

panels.title: 3. Each part guesses separately
panels.caption: Neither module trained for joint questions.

steps.text: Label videos with captions that name exact frame ranges and pixel regions where characters act.

steps.b: Train on spatial and temporal anchors
steps.text: Show the model a caption like "Alice walks right, frames 12–24, pixels 100–200 horizontally" so both location markers and timing markers (the individual pieces of the caption) are tied to the same event.
The model learns that locations and timings are not separate—a character's presence ties location to time.
When asked "where is Alice at 15 seconds," the model reasons across both dimensions at once.
Test on questions that require both spatial and temporal understanding, e.g. "which character moves fastest from left to right after 10 seconds."

object.h2: The single object the paper changes
paras: The object is the training dataset's caption structure. Instead of loose descriptions like "a character walks across the room," each caption now anchors to concrete time intervals and pixel regions: "Frame 12–24, bounding box (x, y, w, h): person walks right."

hidden.h2: Joint localization accuracy: a named hidden quantity
hidden.name: Joint spatial-temporal alignment score
paras: The paper measures a quantity that did not exist before: how well the model pinpoints both where and when in the same answer. This is not spatial accuracy alone (did you find the right pixel?) and not temporal accuracy alone (did you find the right frame?), but the fraction of queries where the model names a location AND a time interval that both match the ground truth.

The paper estimates this by testing on queries designed to require joint reasoning, like "At what frames does Alice sit down?" and "In frame 5, where is Bob?" The metric reports whether the model gives a correct location for the correct time, with no partial credit for getting one right and one wrong.

heat.caption: Darker: higher joint accuracy. Highlighted cells: both spatial and temporal correct on the same query.

reads.html: Think of it as a score from 0 to 100: how often does the model correctly name both the place and the time when asked to find something in a video?
The paper introduces metrics J&F_bi-fore (Jaccard and boundary F-score variants for foreground) to measure alignment on spatial-temporal localization tasks, treating location and time as inseparable.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: grounding teaches binding
paras: The mechanism is surprisingly simple: the model learns only what the data teaches it. In the old regime, a caption like "someone talks" has no timing or location label, so the model has no signal that ties the word "talks" to a specific moment or position—because the data never says "this word goes with this place and time." It treats space and time as independent questions.

When you show the model a caption grounded in both dimensions—"Frame 12–24, box (100, 50, 250, 150): Alice talks"—the model learns that this action happens in a bounded region during a bounded interval. Every word in the caption now has a spatial and temporal anchor. The model gradually internalizes that to answer any question about this action, both dimensions must be checked together. Spatial and temporal information become linked in the model's learned representation.

This changes the model's internal weights (the numbers that encode knowledge). When queried on a new joint question, the weights activate both spatial reasoning and temporal reasoning in parallel, and the model merges the two streams before producing an answer. The binding happens in training, not inference—data with clear joint labels simply shapes the model differently.

stages.s: Video frames and caption with location (box) and time (frame range)
Embed caption tokens with spatial anchors (which pixels)
Embed caption tokens with temporal anchors (which frames)
Learn joint representation: space and time co-occur in training
Model weights encode both dimensions together

math.h2: The loss function for joint grounding
math.words: For each query, the penalty is the sum of spatial mismatch and temporal mismatch. Spatial mismatch is the distance from the predicted box to the true box. Temporal mismatch is the distance from the predicted frame range to the true frame range. The model adjusts its weights to shrink both mismatches at once.
symbols: total penalty the model tries to minimize
Intersection over Union: how much the predicted box overlaps the true box, divided by how much space they cover together
Intersection over Union for time: how much the predicted frame range overlaps the true range, divided by their combined span

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Spatial overlap: pixels in both boxes ≈ 12,000. Total area covered ≈ 20,000. IoU_spatial = 12,000 / 20,000 = 0.6.
Temporal overlap: 11 frames in both ranges. Total range ≈ 14 frames. IoU_temporal = 11 / 14 ≈ 0.79.
Loss = (1 - 0.6) + (1 - 0.79) = 0.4 + 0.21 = 0.61. Model nudges weights to raise both overlaps, lowering the loss.

math.note: The model lowers spatial mismatch and temporal mismatch together during training because both contribute equally to the penalty. If one dimension were weighted more heavily, the model would ignore the lighter dimension in favor of the heavier one.

bars.h2: Comparison: old models vs VideoLoom on joint queries

charts.title: Old Video LLM (space and time separate)
charts.note: Model does well on one dimension at a time, but joint queries require reasoning it was not trained for.

charts.title: VideoLoom (trained jointly)
charts.note: Slight trade-off on single-dimension queries, huge gain on joint reasoning. The trade-off is small because the joint training teaches both dimensions, just with shared structure.

items.html: If captions mislabel where or when (e.g., box is off by 50 pixels or timestamp is wrong by 5 frames), the model learns the wrong joint relationship. The pairing of space and time becomes noisy.

items.b: Characters that move fast or go off-screen confuse the model.
items.html: If a character rapidly changes position, or leaves and re-enters the frame, the model must distinguish separate time periods with the same location. Ambiguous motion patterns weaken the joint signal.
In very long videos, a single bounding box might not cover all instances of a character's action. The joint label becomes approximate, and the model learns a softer binding.

Carefully curate the dataset so each caption's spatial and temporal bounds are tight and unambiguous. Use human review or multi-annotator agreement to catch errors. The tighter the pairing, the stronger the joint learning—because a vague label teaches the model that space and time are loosely related, whereas a precise label teaches tight binding.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple benchmark: take a short video (5–10 seconds) with a single actor. Write 10 queries that require joint reasoning, e.g. 'Where is the actor at frame 5?' and 'When does the actor wave?' and 'During frames 3–7, which hand does the actor raise first?' Train a Video LLM on the script with loose captions (no spatial or temporal grounding), then retrain on captions with precise frame ranges and bounding boxes. Measure how often each version answers the composite queries correctly.
demo.metric_eq: Joint accuracy = (fraction of queries where predicted box AND predicted frame range both match ground truth) × 100
demo.closing: The demo must show a sharp accuracy gain on composite queries when the model trains on jointly grounded captions, even though it stays roughly level on single-dimension queries. That is VideoLoom's proof.
